abstract: >
  We present \pkg{immutables}, an R package providing persistent
  finger-tree-backed collections (catenable sequences, priority queues,
  ordered sequences, and interval indices) with user-extensible monoid
  annotations. The same predicate-based locate and split primitives power
  every built-in operation and remain accessible to users, enabling
  $O(\log n)$ queries over custom aggregates. We describe the API,
  provide micro-benchmarks against base R and existing packages, and
  demonstrate the extension points with a DNA prefix-search example.

# Introduction

The \proglang{R} programming language is a natural first choice for
statistical analyses, but its ever-growing popularity has diversified
its application to domains as broad as web services
\citep{TODO-web-services}, user interfaces
\citep{TODO-user-interfaces}, machine learning
\citep{TODO-machine-learning}, simulation \citep{TODO-simulation},
mobile computing \citep{TODO-rpigpio}, computational geometry
\citep{TODO-comp-geometry}, graph algorithms \citep{TODO-graph-algos},
and much more \citep{TODO-misc-applications}. Data structures, or
collections, are foundational building blocks for almost all computing,
providing the features necessary for efficient in-memory data storage
and retrieval.

Ordinal-indexed arrays, matrices, and lists are ubiquitous in
statistical applications; double-ended queues support fast insertion
and removal from ends and are widely used in state-search and
scheduling applications \citep{TODO-deque-uses}; key-ordered sequences
provide fast search, access, and range queries
\citep{TODO-ordered-sequence-uses}; priority queues associate elements
with priority values for efficient access by minimum or maximum
priority, often used in graph algorithms and simulation
\citep{TODO-pq-uses}. Amongst more exotic structures, pretty trees
find application in bioinformatics \citep{TODO-pretty-trees-bioinf},
and interval trees are widely used in computational geometry
\citep{TODO-interval-tree-geom}.

Data structure implementations generally fall in one of two classes:
mutable or immutable (also known as persistent). Operations on mutable
structures allow the internal structure or contents to change.
Operations on immutable structures, by contrast, return changed copies,
preserving the original for further use. Purely functional languages
like Haskell and ML endorse persistence, and while mutating data
structures are generally easier to implement and faster, the functional
programming community has invested significant effort in designing fast
immutable implementations for a wide variety of applications
\citep{TODO-okasaki}. This immutability is familiar to \proglang{R}
developers, who expect pass-by-value semantics and side-effect-free
functions \citep{TODO-r-semantics}. Most \proglang{R} structures
follow this paradigm, with the exception of index-assignment (e.g.
\code{x[2] <- 4.2}). Even in these cases, \proglang{R}'s
assign-by-value and copy-on-modify semantics ensure safety
(\code{x <- y; x[2] <- 4.2} modifies \code{x} while preserving the
original data in \code{y}).

Unfortunately, native \proglang{R} types do not emphasize
performance -- many operations require a full scan or copy of the
data, making them prohibitively expensive for use in highly dynamic or
large-data applications \citep{TODO-r-perf}. Attempts have been made
to fill these gaps; we previously published an implementation of
efficient, persistent stack and queue structures based on lazy
evaluation techniques (noted as the only use of lazy structures in a
2019 review of the \proglang{R} ecosystem \citep{TODO-2019-review}).
In 2018 T. Barry surveyed the state of collection packages,
identifying 11 packages providing set, map, stack, queue, and/or
sequence structures \citep{TODO-barry-2018}. Of these, only three
implemented side-effect-free structures: \pkg{rstackdeque}
\citep{TODO-rstackdeque}, \pkg{sets} \citep{TODO-sets}, and
\pkg{S4Vectors} \citep{TODO-s4vectors}. The latter two are optimized
for bulk operations as compared to base-\proglang{R} types but, like
\proglang{R} lists and vectors, do not support fast incremental
insert/remove operations. Notably, \pkg{S4Vectors} is designed for
extensibility and is widely used in the Bioconductor ecosystem,
including support for interval ranges via \pkg{IRanges}
\citep{TODO-iranges}. Barry notes a need for fast, flexible, and
side-effect-free data structures to support advanced use cases in the
\proglang{R} ecosystem \citep{TODO-barry-2018}.

Here we describe \pkg{immutables}, which implements a remarkable data
structure known as monoid-annotated 2-3 finger trees. First described
by Hinze and Paterson 20 years ago \citep{hinze2006finger}, these
provide persistent, amortized constant-time access to ends,
$O(\log n)$ search/insertion/removal, and via monoid annotation can
be purposed as other specialized structures
\citep{TODO-finger-tree-applications}. We implement four such
specialized structures: \code{flexseq}s, serving as indexable,
splittable, and concatenable lists with end insertion/removal for
stack and queue operations; priority queues, associating data elements
with priority values for min/max access; ordered sequences, keeping
items in order by provided keys; and interval indices, storing items
with orderable ranges for overlap-like queries. Core operations are
implemented in \proglang{C++} via \pkg{Rcpp} \citep{TODO-rcpp} for
speed, and a developer API is provided to extend functionality via
monoid annotation.

# Overview

## Flexible sequences

At the core of \pkg{immutables} is the \code{flexseq} structure,
which operates similarly to \proglang{R} lists: they can store
elements of any or mixed types, be named, and be indexed with the
familiar \code{[}, \code{[[}, and \code{$} operators with integer, logical, and
name vectors, including replacement. Elements can be inserted, 
accessed, or removed from either end via peek/pop/push operations in 
amortized constant time for efficient double-ended queue behavior. Additionally,
\code{flexseq}s allow concatenation, splitting by position, and
insertions and removals by position in $O(\log n)$ time.

```r
x <- as_flexseq(letters[1:10])
x2 <- push_back(x, "z")
length(x)                 # 10
length(x2)                # 11
x3 <- insert_at(x2, list("p", "q"))
length(x3)                # 13
x4 <- x[1:5]              # flexseq of length 5
result <- pop_back(x3)
result$element            # "z"
result$remaining          # flexseq of length 12
```

Other implemented methods include \code{c()}, \code{as.list()},
\code{unlist()}, \code{fapply()} (analogous to \code{lapply()} for
lists), and \code{print()}, mimicking \code{print.list()} but
displaying only the first and last few elements. Native \proglang{R}
\code{for}-loops do not support iterating over elements as a result
of sequences' internal structure, but \code{loop()} is imported from
the \code{coro} package to support iterative element access.

While \code{flexseq}s support names, these are somewhat limited
compared to named \proglang{R} lists: if names are used, every
element must have a unique non-\code{NULL} name. Further, the usage
of names degrades worst-case performance for some operations to a
full $O(n)$ scan (for example, when concatenating), though front/back
access remains $O(1)$ amortized in named contexts. Otherwise, all
operations are $O(\log n)$ worst case, or $O(k \log n)$ when
deleting $k$ elements. For performance-sensitive applications
requiring named access, ordered sequences (discussed below) can be
associated with character-based names as ordering keys for fast
access.

## Priority queues

The \code{priority_queue} structure stores arbitrary or mixed types, much like
\code{flexseq}, but each element is associated with a priority value.
Rather than efficient front/back access, priority queues provide
efficient ($O(\log n)$) insertion and pop/peek by minimum and maximum
priority value. Priorities may be any orderable type (such as dates),
but full \proglang{C++} optimization is available for primitive
numeric, character, and logical priorities. Because multiple elements
may share the same priority, "all" versus "first" access methods are
available: \code{pop\_all\_min(q)} returns an object with two
priority queues, \code{\$elements} containing all elements with
minimum priority and \code{\$remaining} with the rest
(\code{\$elements} may be easily converted to base \proglang{R} via
\code{as.list()}). Conversely, \code{pop\_min(q)} returns the 
first entry (by insertion order) with minimum priority
in \code{$element}, and the rest of the priority queue in
\code{$remaining}.

```r
q <- as_priority_queue(letters[1:6], priorities = c(2, 1, 3, 1, 9, 7))
peek_min(q)               # "b"
peek_all_min(q)           # priority queue w/ "b" "d"
q2 <- insert(q, "z", priority = 10)
res <- pop_max(q2)
res$element               # "z"
res$remaining             # priority queue w/ 6 entries
```

Internally, elements are stored in insertion order, though this
should not be relied on. Accordingly, priority queues only support
indexing with \code{[}, \code{[[}, and \code{$} by name, with the same caveats
as for named \code{flexseq}s, and replacement indexing with \code{[<-} et al.
is not supported. Priority queues and other advanced types (below) may be 
cast down with \code{as\_flexseq()} and \code{as.list()}, optionally preserving
priority-value metadata. Like \code{flexseq}, priority queues may be mapped
with \code{fapply()}; in this case the called function is supplied both the 
stored element and associated priority value, and returns a priority queue
with identical priority values. Finally, priority queues may be iteratively
accessed in priority order with \code{loop()}, and they additionally 
provide a priority-aware `merge()`.

## Ordered sequences

The \code{ordered_sequence} type associates each element with a key value
and keeps elements in key-value order. Keys may be any orderable
type, with optimizations for primitive types, and duplicate keys are
kept in insertion order. Ordered sequences support efficient insert,
peek, and pop by key, with "all" versions of peek and pop for
edge-case duplicate-key use cases. Ordered sequences also support
key counts and key-range queries.

```r
o <- as_ordered_sequence(letters[1:6], keys = c(20, 10, 30, 10, 90, 70))
peek_key(o, 10)             # "b"
peek_all_key(o, 10)         # ordered sequence w/ "b" "d"
count_key(o, 10)            # 2
elements_between(o, 15, 85) # ordered seq w/ "a" "c" "f"
o2 <- insert(o, "z", key = 100)
res <- pop_key(o2, 100)
res$element                 # "z"
res$remaining               # ordered seq w/ "a" - "f"
```

As with other structures, ordered sequences may be named (the same
name caveats apply) and indexed with \code{[}, \code{[[}, and
\code{$}. Integer indices may be used with \code{[} and \code{[[},
in which case they refer to elements in key-sorted order. When
\code{[} is used to subset an ordered sequence, the return is
another ordered sequence and elements are kept in their original
key-order. A warning is produced if this is not the requested order
(e.g. \code{o[c(2,1)]}). Replacement indexing (\code{[<-} et al.) is not
supported to preserve the key-order invariant.

Also supported are \code{fapply()} (calling
functions accepting elements and keys, returning an ordered sequence),
\code{loop()} (in key order), and key-aware \code{merge()}.
